title: Workshop: Going up
text:
1. A state machine

At every moment, your elevator is in exactly one of five states: IDLE, MOVING, DOORS_OPENING, DOORS_OPEN or DOORS_CLOSING.
Every time round loop(), the code asks: what state am I in, and has anything happened that means I should act or change state? That’s the switch statement in the starter sketch.
A transition is a move from one state to another. It’s triggered by an event (a button press) or a condition (a timer running out, the car reaching a floor).

title: Workshop: Going up
Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 0: Get connected (5 min?)

Open ElevatorStarter.ino in the Arduino IDE and check that ElevatorHAL.h appears as a second tab.
Upload it, then open Tools → Serial Monitor and set it to 115200 baud.
You should see the car on the ground floor and dim landing lights on all three floors.

Done when: pressing each button prints the right floor number.

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 1: Make it move
When a button is pressed and the elevator is IDLE, the car should travel to that floor and stop. Forget the doors for now.
In the input section, if the state is IDLE, set targetFloor, set direction to +1 (up) or -1 (down), and call changeState(MOVING).
In case MOVING:, use the timer pattern to add direction to carPos every MOVE_STEP_MS. When carPos equals hal_floorPosition(targetFloor), change back to IDLE.
Think: what happens if you press the button for the floor you’re already on? What should happen?
Done when: the car glides to whichever floor you ask for, and presses while it’s moving are ignored.

suggested 20 min

title: Workshop: Going up
section: Task 2: Design the doors on paper
text:
Task 2: Design the doors on paper
Before writing any more code, draw a state diagram. Draw all five states as circles. Draw an arrow for every possible transition and label each arrow with the event or condition that causes it.
Your diagram should answer these questions. What must be true before the car is allowed to move? What happens when the doors finish opening, and when they finish closing? Which states need a timer?
Done when: a demonstrator has checked your diagram.

suggested 10 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 3: Build the doors
Change MOVING so that arriving at the target floor opens the doors instead of going straight to IDLE. Then fill in the three door states, following your diagram:

DOORS_OPENING: every DOOR_STEP_MS, add one to doorOpen. When it reaches DOOR_STEPS, go to DOORS_OPEN.
DOORS_OPEN: once DOOR_HOLD_MS has passed, go to DOORS_CLOSING.
DOORS_CLOSING: every DOOR_STEP_MS, subtract one from doorOpen. When it reaches 0, go to IDLE.

Done when: the car arrives, the doors slide open, wait two seconds, then slide shut, and the Serial Monitor shows the whole sequence of states.

suggested 20 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 4: Remember every call
At the moment, anyone who presses a button while the car is busy is ignored. Real elevators remember.
Replace your Task 1 button code with a single line: calls[f] = true; (you’ll see that floor’s landing lights turn blue). Then move the decision-making into case IDLE:. Look for a floor with a call: if it’s the floor the car is already on, clear the call and open the doors; otherwise set targetFloor and direction and start moving. When the car arrives, clear that floor’s call.
Done when: you can press all three buttons quickly and every floor gets visited, with no blue lights left behind.

suggested 15 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 5: Stop on the way
If the car is travelling from floor 0 to floor 2 and someone on floor 1 presses their button in time, the car should stop at floor 1 first.
In MOVING, after each step, use hal_floorAt(carPos) to find out whether the car is level with a floor. If that floor has a call, stop there.
Done when: test scenarios 3 and 4 behave as expected.

suggested 10 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 6: Choose wisely
When several floors are waiting, which should the car visit next? Write a function int chooseNextCall(int here) that returns a floor number, or -1 if nobody is waiting, and use it in IDLE.
Try at least two of these strategies:

Lowest floor first. Simple, but is it fair?
Nearest floor first.
Keep going the same way while anyone is waiting further along in that direction, and only then turn around. This is known as the elevator algorithm (or SCAN).

Discuss with your partner: can you invent a sequence of button presses where somebody waits forever under one of these strategies? Which would you want in a 50-storey building?

suggested 15 min

title: Workshop: Going up
text:
Task 7: Make it safe
Hold the doors. If someone presses the button for the floor the car is stopped at while the doors are closing, open them again. If the doors are already fully open, restart the hold timer so they stay open longer.
Check your invariants. An invariant is something that must always be true, no matter what. After the switch, add checks that print a warning to the Serial Monitor if either of these ever happens: the state is MOVING but doorOpen isn’t 0, or carPos is outside the shaft.
Done when: every scenario in the test table below passes with no warnings.

suggested 15 min

delay(2000) freezes the whole Arduino for two seconds. No buttons are read and no LEDs are updated. An elevator that ignored everyone while its doors were open would be a pretty bad elevator.
Instead, check the clock and only act once enough time has passed:
if (millis() - timer >= MOVE_STEP_MS) {
  timer = millis();   // restart the timer
  // do ONE small step, e.g. move the car by one LED
}
loop() runs thousands of times a second, so lots of tiny steps look like smooth movement, and the buttons get checked between every one of them.

Watch out: store times in unsigned long, never int. On an Arduino Uno an int tops out at 32,767, which is only about 33 seconds’ worth of millis().

title: Architecture overview
text:
Architecture












“Computer architecture, like other architecture, is the art of determining the needs of the user of a structure and then designing to meet those needs as effectively as possible within economic and technological constraints.”
– Frederick P. Brooks


Brooks was an American computer architect, software engineer and computer scientist who managed IBM 360 series of mainframes and their accompanying software.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

A description of a computer (or computer system) which is made from component parts.
Often a high-level description, indicating how components are linked and what each does.
Sometimes includes details such as the instruction set used and other implementation details.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

First documented computer architecture was in correspondence between Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace, where Babbage described his analytical engine.
1936, Conrad Zeus described a computer where both instructions and data are stored in the same memory: First documented instance of a “stored program” or general purpose computer.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

1945, John Von Neumann described the famous Von Neumann Architecture in his paper on the EDVAC computer (successor to the ENIAC).

title: Architecture overview
text:
Computer Architecture

1946, Alan Turing wrote a detailed proposal for the electronic calculator, Automatic Computing Engine, citing Von Neumann.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Von Neumann Architecture


Arrows represent data transfer connections and directions. I.e., there is an arrow in both directions between the memory and the arithmetic logic unit, representing a “shared bus”. We will see later that this shared bus can be a bottleneck.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Store

To store data and instructions. E.g., paper tape, magnetic tape, RAM.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Control Unit

decides which instruction to perform next.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Arithmetic Logic Unit

Performs calculations.

Typically the ALU and control unit are combined into the CPU.
Operations performed on the hardware, or implemented in software.
In early computers, electromechanical hardware was used; these days transistors are used, which require much less energy.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Input and Output

Means for the user to interact with the computer.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Integers

We already saw that an unsigned integer number can be represented in Binary.
Usually the right-most bit represents the least significant digit.
Little-endian representation.
Signed integers may be represented in several ways:

Sign+magnitude: one bit is reserved for the sign, the rest for the value.
This representation allows \(+0\) and \(-0\).
One’s complement: positive numbers represented as usual, negative numbers represented by flipping all their bits.
Again, we have \(+0\) and \(-0\).
Two’s complement: positive numbers represented as usual, negative numbers represented by adding one then flipping all their bits.
only one \(0\), no redundancy.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers

IEEE 754 defines a standard for representing and manipulating floating point numbers.
Represented in a similar way to scientific notation.
E.g., \(300,000,000 = 3 \times 10^8\).

The \(3\) is called the fraction (coefficient or mantissa).
The \(8\) (from \(10^8\)) is called the exponent.

IEEE 754 defines:

The base, typically \(2\) for binary, but sometimes \(10\).
Precision (number of digits to represent the fraction).
An exponent range.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers

Using \(n\) bits, the representation consists of

\(1\) bit for the sign,
\(n - p - 1\) bits for the exponent.
\(p\) bits for the fraction (stored in Binary),

Any signed number up to \(p\) significant digits and a maximum exponent of \(n-p-1\) can be defined.
Positive and negative infinity.
A representation for not a number, e.g., for the result of division by zero.

title: Architecture overview
text:
32-bit floating point
Representation used for the float type in many programming languages.


\(32\) bits:

\(1\) bit for the sign,
\(8\) bits for the exponent,
\(23\) bits for the fraction.

Around \(7\) decimal digits for the fraction.
A double uses \(64\) bits, \(52\) bits (around \(16\) decimal digits).

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point numbers
Advantages

Efficient representation of very large and very small numbers.
Fast computation due to many years of hardware development.

Disadvantages

Floating point errors.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Precision and accuracy

Precision: how many significant digits,
Accuracy: how close to the true value.

A value may be precise but not accurate, accurate but not precise, or both inaccurate and imprecise.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Floating point errors

We know that \(1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1\).
However, \(0.3333333333 + 0.3333333333 + 0.3333333333 = 0.9999999999\)!
\(1/10\) is easy to represent in decimal: \(0.1\).
However, in binary, it is \(0.001100110011\).
Floating point representation is sufficient for most applications, e.g., 3D games.
However, we have to take care with things like currency, which must be correct.

The ENIAC (1945)


Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer

Special purpose computer for artillery firing table calculations.
Located at the School of Engineering and Applied Science, Pennsylvania State University














Could be “programmed” by using the plug-board and switches, data entered via punched cards.
Later converted into a stored program computer.
Base-10 arithmetic instead of the usual binary.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Colossus (1943-45)













Special purpose computer developed at Bletchley Park to help break the Lorenz cipher.
Designed by Tommy Flowers, a research engineer at the General Post Office, based on plans by Code and Cipher School mathematician Max Newman.




Used vacuum tubes; programmed using switches and a plug board.
Data memory was a cycling strip of paper tape.
Colossus Mk II, which used shift registers to run 6 times faster, went into operation in time for the D-day landings.
By the end of the war, 10 Colossi were in operation.

title: Architecture overview
text:
General purpose computers (post WW2)
Von Neumann arranged a 6-week summer workshop to design and build a new type of computer.

General purpose: many early computers were designed with a specific task in mind, which meant they were difficult to repurpose.
Von Neumann wanted to build a stored program computer.
Electronic:replacing electromechanical components which were brittle, hot and noisy.
Colossus and the ENIAC both consumed 150KW of power.
Use binary, which is the easiest encoding to work with when using electronic components.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Maurice Wilkes

Cambridge mathematician, physics PhD on “radio propagation of very long radio waves in the ionosphere”.
Attended Jon Neumann’s workshop, then returned to Cambridge to build the EDSAC machine.
Worked in radar during WW2, which inspired the memory technology for EDSAC.
Memory was a limitation for early electronic computers, Wilkes used “delay lines”, mercury tubes and an oscilloscope, as memory.


More information on mercury delay lines: Radar pulses were captured and played as sound waves. Sound waves passed through mercury, which slowed them down. Picked up by a microphone and displayed no an oscilloscope screen. Sound wave amplified and played back through the speaker so the pulse would repeat as long as needed.

title: Architecture overview
text:
EDSAC (6 May 1949)


Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator

One of the first stored program computers which used binary.
Developed by Maurice Wilkes, William Renwick (hardware engineer) and David Wheeler (first system software engineer).














Could perform 700 additions or 200 multiplications per second.
512 18-bit words of memory for programs and data, upgraded to 1024 18-bit words in 1952.
Data and programs were loaded via 5-hole punched paper tape, initial orders instructed the computer to load the program.
Consumed 11KW of power.
The delay line memory was sub-optimal, but one of the best options at the time.
Although the words were 18-bits, only 17 bits were used in practice owing to unreliability of memory. ## Programming the EDSAC
Programs designed on paper and then punched, in assembler, onto 5-hole paper tape. Programmers became proficient at reading programs from the tape.
Programmers would hang their tape on a line, waiting for an operator to run them – the first “job queue”.
Operator would load program and data and then either return the printed output or inform the programmer of the memory address at which the program failed. ## Operating EDSAC
Built-in add, multiply, bus and conditional jump.

No load. Instead, Instead clear the register (set to \(0\)) and add the value from memory to the register.
No division, but it was included as a subroutine.

In case of a program error, the operator would inform the programmer at which address their program failed.
There was no debugger. An oscilloscope screen showed the state of the registers, and a speaker played a different note depending on the value of the accumulator register. An experienced programmer learnt the sound of a failing program, e.g., if there was an infinite loop. ## Operating EDSAC
Programmers had to use “bad” programming technique. E.g., to access a different array element, the code would modify itself to point to the correct address.
No built-in mechanism for subroutines, instead perform a Wheeler jump: Jump with return memory address, computer would modify the last instruction of the subroutine to jump back to this return address.- No recursion was possible on the EDSAC. Turing proposed the call stack in his 1945 paper, which implemented subroutines “properly” and allowed recursion.

title: Architecture overview
text:
Usage
A condition for funding was that EDSAC must provide a service, as opposed to just being an engineering experiment.

Ronald Fisher, with Wilkes and Wheeler, used EDSAC to solve a differential equation for gene frequency – first use of computers in biology.
In 1951, Miller and Wheeler computed a 79-digit prime number, the largest known at its time.
EDSAC played a role in Nobel-prize-winning research: Nobel laureates thanked EDSAC in their acceptance speech. John Kendrew and Max Perutz (Chemistry, 1962), Andrew Huxley (Medicine, 1963) and Martin Ryle (Physics, 1974)
EDSAC remained in operation until 11 July 1958, when it was superseded by EDSAC 2, which ran until 1965.

Learning Outcomes

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Optimising the fetch-decode-execute-store cycle

Suppose the CPU can perform one stage per CPU cycle.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Von Neumann architecture is sequential

Suppose the computer can perform one stage per CPU cycle.
The ALU is only working during the Execute stage.
It would be ideal to have the ALU doing work all the time.
We’ll look at three ways of getting the best use out of the hardware.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipelines
Overlap stages of the fetch-decode-execute-store cycle.

ALU receives a constant stream of work.

Instruction pipelining is a bit like a production line. Each piece of hardware has its designated job – Control unit for decoding, ALU for executing. Once an instruction is decoded, it is passed to the ALU for execution, while the ALU executes the instruction, the Control unit is decoding the next. This means the ALU is not sitting idle while the control unit decodes instructions for it.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Speedup
In a sequential fetch, decode, execute, store cycle, it takes 4 cycles for each instruction to complete.

40 cycles for 10 instructions.
In a pipelined architecture:

It takes 4 cycles for the first instruction to exit the pipeline.
5 cycles for the second
6 for the third,
… and so on …
14 for the 10-th instruction to exit the pipeline.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Speedup
\[
S_n = \dfrac{\text{Time to complete } n \text{ tasks sequentially}}{\text{Time to complete} n \text{ tasks in a pipeline}}
\]

The speedup for 10 instructions in a 4 stage pipeline is \[
S_10 = \dfrac{40}{14} \approx 2.86
\]
The more instructions, the better! \[
S_{100} = \dfrac{400}{104} \approx 3.51, S_{1000} = \dfrac{1000}{1014} = 3.94
\]

For a pipeline with \(k\) stages, speedup approaches \(k\) as the number of instructions grows very large.

Mathematical explanation:

Suppose we have \(n\) instructions to complete.
For a pipeline with \(k\) stages:

The first operation leaves the pipeline after \(k\) cycles.
The \(n\)-th instruction leaves the pipeline after \(k + n\) cycles.

\(T_{\mathrm{pipeline}} = k + n\) CPU cycles.
Without pipelining, each stage is completed sequentially for each instruction.
\(T_{\mathrm{seq}} = k \cdot n\) CPU cycles.
We can calculate speedup, a measure of how much quicker the pipelines system is: \[S = \dfrac{T_{\mathrm{seq}}}{T_{\mathrm{pipeline}}} = \dfrac{k \cdot n}{k + n}.\]
Pipelines work best for a large number of tasks: \(n \gg k\).
Then \(S = k\).

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Throughput and latency

Throughput: Number of instructions completed per unit time.

\(\text{Throughput} = \dfrac{\text{number of instructions}}{\text{execution time}}\)
Higher throughput indicates better performance.

Latency: time taken for a single instruction to complete (travel through the pipeline)

\(\text{Latency} = \dfrac{\text{execution time}}{\text{number of instructions}}\)
Lower latency indicates better performance.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipelines


Advantages

Higher throughput: more instructions per second
Better hardware utilisation: reduces idle time.
Well-suited to repetitive tasks.


Disadvantages

Higher latency: time taken to complete one instruction
More complex: increases design complexity, manufacture cost and, therefore, time.
Works most efficiently when kept full.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Pipeline hazards

Situations which cause the pipeline to stall, or have to restart.
Control dependency: which instructions should be pipelines after a jump?
Data hazards: when data dependence affecting instructions at different stages of the pipeline.

One instruction may depend on the result of a previous instruction still in the pipeline.
Read after write: one instruction attempts to read data which another instruction has not yet written.
Write after read: one instruction writes data after another instruction attempts to read it.
Write after write: one instruction attempts to write data after another, messing up register values.




control dependency: after a jump instruction, instructions may need to be loaded from a new location of memory. It is unknown, at the time the jump enters the pipeline, what its outcome will be, therefore the correct sequence of instructions cannot be pipelines.

Processors employ branch prediction to guess whether a jump is likely to happens or not. The “most likely” sequence of instructions are pipelined, meaning there is a high probability that the correct instructions are loaded into the pipeline. However, if branch prediction is incorrect, then the pipeline must be restarted, as different instructions need to be fetched, decoded, etc.

Data dependencies: one instruction may depend upon the result of another, so it must wait (stall) until its dependant has left the pipeline. Now we have a “bubble” (empty gap) in the pipeline.

There may be contention over registers wherein one instruction attempts to read or write to registers, or cache, being used by another. In this case, a calculation may have to be restarted, or at least the correct data loaded from memory (slowwww) again.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Reservation station and reorder buffer

Some CPUs have multiple ALUs, or special-purpose hardware.
We want all of this hardware to be working all of the time.
However, we need to figure out which operations can be re-ordered or executed in parallel.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Example: Euclidean distance

Suppose we have two points, \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) in 2d space, e.g., in a 2d game.
To calculate the distance between \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1,x_2)\) and \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1,y_2)\), we use Pythagoras’ theorem.
Euclidean distance, \(D = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\).
Let \(x_1 = 4, x_2 = 9, y_1 = 20, y_2 = 11\).


Don’t worry about the actual formula. It’s only important to note we have a square root, two multiplications, and an addition.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Sequential calculation
CPU can add, mul, sub and sqrt in a single CPU cycle.

t1 = x2 - x1
t2 = t1 * t1
t3 = y1 - y2
t4 = t3 * t3
`t5 = t2 + t4’
D = sqrt( t5 )

6 CPU cycles.

Note: sqrt is a relatively complex operation for computers and some CPUs do not include it as an instruction. However, many CISC (complex) architectures do.

title: Pipelines, Out Of Order Execution, and Parallelism
text:
Parallel calculation
Now suppose we have 2 ALUs.

t1 and t3 can be computed
Given t1 and t3, t2 and t4 respectively can be computed in parallel.
t5 must wait for t2 and t4,
The result, D depends on t5.

… but how can the CPU, a clump of transistors, figure this out?

title: The CPU
text:
Recap: Harvard architecture


Recall the control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output. Harvard architecture has separate memory for programs and data, and a separate bus. This meant there was less contention as instructions and data could be accessed simultaneously, but the machine was less flexible, e.g., the program memory may not be full when data memory is, but we cannot use the free space in the program memory for additional data. This architecture commonly used in embedded systems, and mainframes.

title: The CPU
text:
The Von Neumann Architecture


Same components: control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output. In the Harvard architecture, data and instructions are stored in the same memory. A single memory bus can be a bottleneck, and concerns were raised about security (e.g., a program can write to any location in memory, including modifying the instructions. Simpler and more flexible. This is the architecture found in most desktop computers today.

title: The CPU
text: Components

title: The CPU
text:
The CPU

A program, written in assembler, is a sequence of instructions.
The program is loaded into main memory so that the next instruction is in the next memory address:

title: The CPU
text:
The CPU
the program counter (PC) points to the memory location of the current instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
The CPU

The current instruction itself is stored in the instruction register (IR).

title: The CPU
text:
The CPU

The control unit decodes the instruction and tells the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) which operations to perform.

title: The CPU
text:
The CPU

The CPU has a small number of registers (R1, R2, and R3 on the picture) to store intermediate values.
There is also a small amount of very fast memory, the cache, located either on or very near the CPU.

title: The CPU
section: The Fetch, decode, execute store Cycle
text:
The Fetch, decode, execute store Cycle
A CPU goes through four stages to run an instruction:

title: The CPU
text:
Fetch



First stage of the cycle.
Program counter points to the memory address of the next instruction.
Retrieve the next instruction from memory and store it in the instruction register.
Increment the program counter to point to the next instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
Decode



The control unit reads the current instruction in the instruction register.
The control unit determines which operation(s) to perform.
If the instruction has operands the control unit initiates additional fetches to retrieve these from memory.











The CPU is now ready to execute the instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
Execute



The stage at which operations are performed.
The ALU performs the decoded operation with its operands.
In more advanced CPUs may have special-purpose hardware, e.g., a floating point unit.
Instruction may load data from memory into a register.
May perform a jump (e.g., conditional or loop) – program counter is set to point to a different instruction.











Any return value is stored in a register. Ready for the next stage…

title: The CPU
text:
Interrupt

Occasionally, the CPU receives an interrupt signal.
The CPU immediately stops executing the current instruction and jumps to an interrupt service routine.
The interrupt service routine is just another set of instructions stored in memory.
The CPU executes these instructions as usual, then jumps back to the instruction it was previously working on.
If the instruction was interrupted halfway through, then the CPU must restart it from the beginning.

title: The CPU
text:
The Little man Computer



Simple model of a Von Neumann architecture computer.
Imagine a “Little Man” trapped inside a locked mail room.
The mail room has 100 mailboxes labelled 00-99, each of which can hold a 3 decimal digit instruction or data.












Input is received via an inbox and output returned via an outbox.
There is a work area with a simple addition and subtraction, the accumulator.
There is a program counter which tells the Little Man from which address to fetch the next instruction.

title: The CPU
text:
How it works

The Little Man checks the program counter and retrieves the instruction at the specified address.
The program counter is incremented so that it points to the address (mailbox) containing the next instruction.
Little Man decodes the instruction.


Op-code: number from 000-999 which tells the Little Man what operation to perform.
If data is required, its mailbox address is included in the instruction.


If required, data is fetched from the mailbox referred in the instruction.
Execute the instruction.
Branch (change the value in the program counter) or store the result of the instruction.
Repeat or halt.

Since instructions are stored in mailboxes, they can be labelled, too.
E.g., loop OUT labels the location of the OUT instruction as loop.

E.g., BNP loop goes to loop as long as the accumulator value is positive.
A labelled mailbox can be initialised to a constant.
E.g., one DAT 1 initialises the mailbox labelled one to \(1\).

title: The CPU
text:
Instruction set architectures

Each processor architecture has its own instruction set:
A set of op-codes which the control unit interprets as instructions.
There are two main types of instruction set architecture

RISC: reduced instruction set computer, and
CISC: complex instruction set computer.

title: The CPU
text:
History

Up to the early 80’s, more instructions were being added to processors.
Designers wanted to mimic high-level programming languages.
One CPU instruction should be one line of source code.
Offload more work onto the hardware.
Produce shorter programs (fewer total instructions) to conserve memory.

title: The CPU
text:
History

In the early 80’s, the idea of creating a smaller and simple set of instructions was proposed.
Aim was to make designing and building a CPU easier, cheaper and, therefore, faster.
Term RISC coined by David Patterson, a researcher at UC Berkeley.

title: The CPU
text:
RISC: reduced instruction set computer
Small, simple set of instructions, e.g., as found in the Little Man computer.

Processor can execute exactly one instruction per cycle.
Instructions are a fixed length (fixed number of bits).
Can only manipulate values stored in CPU registers.
RISC chips are simple to design and cheap to build.
Used in ARM-based chips, found in microcontrollers (Arduino, Raspberry Pi) and smartphones.
Also used in IBM Power processors (used in mainframes and servers).

title: The CPU
text:
CISC: complex instruction set computing
Large number of instructions, some performing more complicated operations – intended to correspond to statements in a high-level programming language.

Variable-length instructions.
May take multiple clock cycles to execute an instruction.
Able to manipulate values directly in main memory.
CISC chips are complex, with special-purpose hardware, and are more expensive to build.
Found in most PCs – the x86 architecture.

title: The CPU
text:
Simple example: RISC vs CISC
Suppose we want to increment a value stored in main memory.

title: The CPU
text:
CISC architecture

A single instruction:
ADD mem one

Retrieves the value from memory,
Adds one to it,
Writes back to memory.


CISC architecture

Three separate instructions:
LDA mem
ADD one
STA mem

title: The CPU
text:
Second-generation of computers

Recall that early computers, e.g., EDSAC, used vacuum tubes (thermionic valves).
These were bulky, unreliable, generated lots of heat and required lots of energy to run.
In the late 1950s, computers began to use electronic circuit boards made out of transistors instead.
These computers were popular until the late 1960s.

title: The CPU
text:
First transistor computer



Developed at the University of Manchester
Working prototype in November 1953,
had 92 transistors and 950 diodes.
Full-size version was operational in 1955
had 200 transistors, 1300 diodes and consumed 150W of power.
Early transistors were unreliable. Average error-free runtime was 1.5 hours.
Not fully transistorised as it still used vacuum tubes in its clock.












TRADIC transistor computer, developed at Bell Labs, released January 1954.
Used a single high-power output vacuum tube amplifier to obtain a 1MHz clock speed.

title: The CPU
text:
Fully transistorised computer

Harwell Cadet, 1955. 58KHz clock speed.
Prototype IBM 604 Transistor calculator.
IBM 608, released April 1955 is considered to be the first commercial fully solid-state transistor computer.

title: The CPU
text:
Third generation computers

Widely used from the mid 60s to early 70s.
Used integrated circuits (ICs)
An IC is a single chip containing all transistors, resistors, capacitors, diodes and connections needed to operate.
Invented by Jack Kilby in 1958, an electrical engineer working at Texas Instruments.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.
Faster and more reliable than second generation.
Reduced computing time from micro seconds to nano seconds.
Computers were becoming more compact, affordable and easy to use with high-level programming languages and mouse and keyboard instead of punched cards.

title: The CPU
text:
Moore’s “Law”

Prediction made by Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, in 1965:
“Number of transistors per chip doubles every two years.”


Note that it’s not a “law” as in “law of physics”. More of a prediction which has remained (mostly) true.

title: The CPU
text: Moore’s Law Graph

title: The CPU
text:
Dennard scaling

Stated in a 1974 paper co-authored by Robert H. Dennard:
“As transistors get smaller, their power density stays constant – power use stays in proportion with area.”
If a transistor is 30% smaller, then its power consumption is 30% less.
An IC of fixed size with twice the number of transistors consumes the same power.
Allowed manufacturers to significantly increase clock speed without increase power consumption.

title: The CPU
text:
Dennard scaling



Appears to have broken down since 2006.
Since 2016 the number of transistors per chip is still growing, but more slowly.
As transistors get smaller, current leakage and heat production is more problematic.












We see clock speed plateau – as clack speed increases it becomes more difficult to cool the chip.
This is called the power wall.

title: The CPU
text:
Exercise: Moore’s law
Discuss:

Is Moore’s law still true today?



There have been many predictions of the death of Moore’s law.
We are no longer able to double the number of transistors per chip.
Transistors are still getting smaller and more tightly packed, but progress is becoming slower.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Learning Outcomes

Describe the purpose of an operating system.
Use a layered model to explain what is, and is not, in the scope of an operating system.
Overview computer history in the context of operating systems, and use this to explain why the functions of an operating system are important.

title: Operating Systems
text:
What is an Operating System

Just another program.
Provides a programming interface for the computer hardware.
Responsible for managing (protecting) resources.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Managing resources

Typically hardware, e.g.,
CPU, memory, files on disk, peripherals.
Resources are limited.

embedded devices and smart devices still have small amounts of memory,
even large supercomputers are not powerful enough for scientists,
modern PCs have huge amounts of memory and processing power compared to early computers.
Many users still want more, e.g., for smooth game performance.

Resources need protecting.

title: Operating Systems
section: What protection should the OS provide?
text:
What protection should the OS provide?

Security and integrity
Prevent one user or program from corrupting another.
Authorisation
Ensures only those “allowed” have access to certain resources.
Authentication
Checking whether a user or program has the authorisation it claims to have.
Save me from myself
Protecting the user / programmer from their own stupid mistakes.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Optimise performance

In addition, operating systems ensure resources meet certain criteria.
E.g.,:

responsiveness: by prioritising certain events,
real-time: such as machinery in a factory, actuators on an aircraft,
security: by preventing accidental or malicious tampering.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Programming interface

Easier access to hardware and peripherals:
hardware programming can be fiddly and complicated.
Less repeated code:
Common tasks, e.g., file handling, are implemented.
Less chance of errors

Since the OS is written by experts.
Code is used by many people, so there is more chance of errors being found and fixed.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Written by experts

Experts understand the hardware:

understand exactly how the hardware works,
know how to get the best performance,
know the intricacies and pitfalls of hardware programming,
consider all the details, e.g., handling interrupts,




Device drivers were probably written by the hardware manufacturers themselves.
We can safely assume that expert OS developers are better programmers, and better computer scientists than us.
They likely already made most of the mistakes, and learnt from them, that less experienced programmers are likely to make.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Layered model













Splits a computer system into distinct chunks,
which interact with each other through and interface.
Modelling allows us to look at the system in an appropriate level of detail.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Layered model



Hardware: warm scone,
Cream: user-land applications, including the GUI.
Jam: operating system, providing an insulating layer between the scone and cream.
Protects the hardware from user-land applications.











A computer, applications and its operating system is like a correctly constructed scone.



We represent a computer, applications and operating system as a 3-layered model
Analogy: a correctly constructed scone. Note that jam is a good insulator and prevents the warm scone from causing the cream to melt.
Thus the OS is like the jam.

title: Operating Systems
section: Note: GUI is a user-land application
text:
Note: GUI is a user-land application

Any program the user interacts with is not part of the operating system
this is “user-land”.
The GUI (desktop environment, window manager, etc) is not part of the operating system.
As computer scientists, we should not confuse

the OS and its GUI,
the OS and the hardware it is running on.




Many people confuse the OS and the GUI, and OS and the hardware it runs on.
OS manufacturers contribute to this confusion by marketing the GUI / hardware as part of the OS.
E.g., think of Windows advertisements which emphasise the GUI, or Mac advertisements which emphasise the Apple hardware.
However, if you’ve ever used Linux, you may have come across different “flavours” of the same distribution, which include different desktop environments (GUIs).
You may also be familiar with the same OS running on different hardware. E.g., running Windows on Mac hardware, running Linux on Mac or PC hardware.
Thus, as computer scientists, we need to be clear about what the OS is:
the layer between the hardware and user-land, responsible for managing and protecting resources, as well as providing an interface to the programmer.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Separation of concerns

Layering allows us to decouple software:

device drivers (e.g., interacting with peripherals),
OS code (e.g., process scheduling, memory management),
and user interface

should be as loosely coupled as possible.



loose coupling: means the code of different components is intertwined as little as possible.
in a loosely coupled system, you should be able to swap out one component for another without needing to make many changes to the rest of the system.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Tight coupling causes problems



Huge source of bugs,
since an error in the GUI could cause the entire system to crash.
Security risk
as a malicious user could gain access to OS internals through a poorly programmed application.











The famous “blue screen of death”.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Loose coupling enables code re-use



Loose coupling allows us to swap out one component,
while making minimal changes to the rest of the system.
This allows us to re-use much of the OS code, while only changing hardware-specific drivers,
allowing the same OS to run on many devices.

The Android OS shares lots of code with the Linux kernel.

title: Operating Systems
section: A good operating system should be…
text:
A good operating system should be…

Lightweight and efficient
so that as many resources as possible can be dedicated to user-land applications.
Flexible and easy to use,
i.e., it should be a help, not a hindrance, to the programmer.

title: Operating Systems
section: Early computers did not have operating systems
text:
Early computers did not have operating systems


Programs loaded into EDSAC from paper tape,
“starting orders” helped the operator load and initialise the program.
Programmer had to know which machine they were writing code for
since each early computer was slightly different.
Had to write low-level code, interacting directly with the hardware,
e.g., each program re-implemented printing to the TTY.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Manual scheduling


Each program (job) was hung on a line,
forming a job queue.
A human operator manually loaded each program into the computer,
If the program ran successfully, its output would be returned to the programmer,
In case of an error, the operator would write the memory address at which the program failed and return this to the programmer.
Turn-around could be days, if there was an error the programmer would have to restart the process.












In the 60s, there was no such thing as hacking away at a program and re-running it until it worked. Programmers learnt to “run” the programs in their heads, read machine code from paper tape, understand oscilloscope traces or audio cues to determine if their program was running correctly. At this time there were no high-level languages, and no debuggers.

title: Operating Systems
section: Code re-use: libraries and device drivers
text:
Code re-use: libraries and device drivers

Early programmers had to re-implement everything.

writing output,
working with files,
performing maths operations such as square root.

Libraries were soon developed, so that programmers could share commonly repeated code.
To avoid low-level programming, working directly with hardware, device drivers were developed.
Linkers and loaders were then developed to give access to this shared code.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Spooling

Early computers were expensive to run.
So it was important to keep the CPU as busy as possible.
Manually loading programs became a bottleneck.
A batch of programs was loaded onto a “fast” medium (magnetic tape) and run sequentially.
This process was called spooling.
Printing output via a teleprinter was also a bottleneck,
so this was also spooled.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Monitor

A small program which

loaded a program,
ran it on the hardware,
and wrote its output.

Directed by a special-purpose programming language called job control language.
See e.g., IBM JCL, or SLURM.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Monitor

Also responsible for automatic accounting, prioritising e.g., users who paid more and killing processes if they exceeded allocated CPU or memory.
Still widely used in modern mainframes or time-shared supercomputers.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Multitasking

Some operations were slow and needed no CPU,
e.g., writing output.
To best utilise the CPU, multiple programs were loaded at once,
When the CPU was idle, another program could make use of it.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Multitasking

The Monitor was responsible for scheduling the programs,
i.e., deciding which should be run and when.
Note that exactly one program ran at a time.
Each program had to surrender control back to the monitor,
there was no way for the Monitor to automatically stop a rogue program.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Co-operative approach

Several programs and their data were loaded into memory.
All programs, including the Monitor, had the same rights.
One program was able to

monopolise resources by not surrendering control,
overwrite another program or its data,
overwrite the Monitor.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Early scheduling

Monitor allowed one program to run until it surrendered control.
Problem: a malicious or erroneous program could monopolise all resources.
More complicated scheduling algorithms were suggested,
but these consumed valuable resources, so simplicity was preferred.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Early scheduling

Another approach: pre-emptive scheduling.
The Monitor regularly interrupted running processes and decided what to do. I.e.,

continue running the same process,
run a different process,
kill the process if it had consumed too many resources.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Pre-emptive scheduling

More frequently:

each program gets a small slice of CPU,
appears more responsive,
lots of time spent handling interrupts, less time running user programs,
each interrupt “wakes up” the CPU, which consumes excessive power (in low-power systems where the CPU is often idle).

title: Operating Systems
text:
Pre-emptive scheduling

Less frequently:

programs appear slow, do not respond to user interactions,
compute intensive programs run bets, having more CPU time and less context switching,
less time spent running the monitor.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Thrashing

When a computer spends all its time running the Monitor and deciding what to do.
This was a common problem in early operating systems.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Potential solution

Use unequal time slices:

larger and less frequent slices given to compute-intensive programs.
smaller and more frequent slices given to interactive programs.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Resource protection

Early programs had the same rights:
everyone had equal access to all hardware.
Protection was needed,
this required hardware support.
CPU instructions were divided into two or more levels:

Unprivileged: “safe” instructions which all programs could run,
Privileged: e.g., access to peripherals, scheduling a process.

Only the Monitor could run in privileged mode.

title: Operating Systems
text:
User-land programs in privileged mode

If a user-land application tries to run a privileged operation,

CPU jumps to the Monitor,
monitor decides what to do,
perhaps allow the instruction, or kill the process if it is not allowed.

A user-land program may “politely ask” to perform a privileged operation,
by raising a system call (syscall).

title: Operating Systems
text:
Memory protection

All programs had equal access to memory.
one program could overwrite another program or its data,
or overwrite prat of the Monitor.
Protection was needed,
and this also required hardware support.
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) was responsible for this.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Memory Management Unit

Memory divided into “pages”, typically 4096 bytes, but often larger, e.g., 4MB.
For each program, MMU stores a table of pages,
for each address, the MMU has a flag indicating whether the program can

read,
write,
or execute (run as code)

that page.

title: Operating Systems
text:
The Memory Management Unit

It is useful to separate reading, writing and executing.

Prevents one program overwriting another program or its data,
Prevents user data being treated as code (security risk),

title: Operating Systems
text:
Fast and transparent

Each access to memory must be checked by the MMU,
If a program attempts to access memory out of bounds, an interrupt is sent to the OS,
which typically kills the process (through raising a segmentation fault SIGSEGV).
this is yet another overhead. MMU must be very fast and operate transparently.

title: Operating Systems
text:
Late 60s to mid 90s

Pre-emptive scheduling and resource protection began to appear in mainframes in the late 1960s.
DOS (Disk OS), an early “home” OS was a single program OS with no pre-emption or memory protection due to lack of hardware support.
Windows 3.1 also had no pre-emption or memory protection.
Hardware support was quickly added,
by the mid 80s, Unix-derived OSs added pre-emption and memory protection.

title: Operating Systems
section: Summary: what have early computers taught us?
text:
Summary: what have early computers taught us?

Resources need managing,
since they are limited, we want to get best performance otu of hardware and best user experience.
Resources also need protection
from out or malicious programs, e.g., limiting access to memory, but also files and network.
Programmers need a convenient interface,
to best interact with hardware, avoid repeating code, and produce fewer errors.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Latches

Component which “remembers” a value until it is changed by a new signal.
Can be used to store \(1\) bit of data.
Widely used in digital circuits, e.g., for data storage, control and flip-flop circuits.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch



Set-reset latches are the simplest type of latch.
Can be constructed from two NOR gates.
Two inputs, \(S\) (set) and \(R\) (reset). State is changed when a pulse (high voltage, or \(1\)) is applied to \(S\) or \(R\).
The output is \(Q\) and its inverse is \(\overline{Q}\).

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch












Initial state: no voltage to \(S\) or \(R\).



\(Q\) shows \(1\), its inverse, \(\overline{Q}\) shows \(0\).
To reset, apply a pulse to \(R\).
\(Q\) set to \(0\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(1\).
To set the latch, apply a pulse to \(S\).
\(Q\) is set \(1\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(0\).
Applying a pulse to both \(Q\) and \(R\) is not valid.

Gated SR latch



We may only want the state to change if the latch is enabled.
This can be done by building a gated latch.
Recall that an AND gate is only true when both inputs are true.
So we add AND gates, creating another input, \(E\).



The state can only change if \(E\) has a high voltage applied to it.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Application: switch bounce

Latches are widely used in electrical engineering as well as electronic computers.
When a mechanical switch is pressed, it may cause several pulses to be sent.
An SR-latch ensures that only one signal is sent, since subsequent pulses to \(S\) or \(R\) will not cause a change in state.

A gated latch can be used when state should only be changed when a device is Enabled.



E.g., an air conditioning unit may switch cooling on and off depending on input from a temperature sensor, but the unit should only switch on cooling if it has been turned on by the user.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
D-latch



0Data or transparent latches have two inputs: Data (\(D\)) and Enable (\(E\)).
The state changes to the value of \(D\) only when \(E\) signal is high.
When the Enable signal is low, the value of \(D\) is stored until the leading edge of the next rising Enable Signal.



A D-latch can be built from a gated SR-latch.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Flip-flops

Latches are inexpensive and easy to implement using simple logic components.
However, their behaviour can be unpredictable owing to a lack of synchronisation.
Flip-flops add a clack to synchronise their operaton.
A gated latch can be converted into a flip-flop by connecting a clock to the Enable input.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
JK Flip-flops



Reset: high pulse to \(K\).
Set: high pulse to \(J\).
If a high pulse is sent to both \(J\) and \(K\), then the state is toggled.
I.e., \(0\) becomes \(1\) and \(1\) becomes \(0\).











We can use the above to build a counter.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Counting in binary

We saw that digital circuits have two possible values: low (or \(0\)) and high (or \(1\)).
Everything (letters, images, sounds, programs) in a computer is represented by a number.
Numbers are encoded in binary using a certain number of binary digits (bits).
A whole (integer) number is typically represented using \(8\) bits (a byte).
E.g., for unsigned (\(\ge 0\)) integers, \(0 = 00000000\), \(37 = 00100101\).
